     "subtitle": "Pluralism without dazzling coalitions: seeking a civilizational minimum",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić in the studio, in frame with the episode caption „Oko ovoga se ljevičari i desničari MORAJU slagati!“ and the logo of Mladi za Domovinu.",
     "content": "Episode 115 of the podcast of the association **Mladi za Domovinu** opens with a thesis on political pluralism, which is often praised in Croatia as a value. Host **Marin Marić** recalls that the number of political parties increases after every election cycle, while political discourse is increasingly „poisoned“ and reduced to base passions. For precisely this reason, as he states, there is a lack of basic shared premises about Croatian politics.\n\nMarić announces that with guest **Petar Šarić** he will try to define the „civilizational minimums“ that Croatian politics should respect so that pluralism can truly live. He emphasizes that they are not seeking dazzling coalitions or politicians of opposing worldviews walking together. The goal is to determine a framework within which parties may sharply disagree, but with the conviction that certain fundamental rules are respected.\n\nThe conversation follows on from Šarić’s column on environmental protection and political ideologies, in which he also touched on the topic of contra-arianism, that is, a positioning defined exclusively against the other side. Marić points out that worldview consistency in the age of mass media suffers from the oversaturation of the media space and from the strategies of political elites and propagandists who opportunistically exploit this situation.",

     "content": "Host Marin Marić introduces the guest as his friend, a philosopher and sociologist, a doctoral student at the Faculty of Philosophy in Ljubljana.      "subtitle": "Principles instead of counter-positioning: environmental protection as an objective foundation",
     "screenshot_description": "Petar Šarić explains the difference between principles and reactive opposition, with a hand gesture as he speaks.",
     "content": "In answer to Marić’s question of what it means to be positioned only against the other side of the spectrum, Šarić replies that in the age of political postmodernity great narratives and great ideologies have been lost. As a result, people lose the orientation of their own worldview, so that they may one day argue one claim and ten days later its complete opposite, simply because the advocate of some idea is unpleasant to them or belongs to another circle.\n\nŠarić advocates that in politics and public advocacy we orient ourselves more toward principles and less toward the comfort of belonging. As an example he cites environmental protection. From the perspective of a patriotic position, he argues, environmental protection makes sense as a principle that should be established and advocated, regardless of the fact that a certain political current has appropriated this topic.\n\nŠarić adds that the courage to hold to objective principles is important even when ideologies go in directions that may place an individual on the wrong side in relation to the normative expectations of their own group.",

     "subtitle": "City government in Zagreb: is a good thing good regardless of who does it?",
     "screenshot_description": "Footage of the Zagreb urban area, with indications of projects such as the stadium on Kranjčevićeva and the railway line.",
     "content": "As an example of reflexive opposition, Marić cites a situation in which every move of the Zagreb city government is met with criticism, even when it is objectively positive. He mentions the planned decent stadium on Kranjčevićeva and the extension of the railway line, which, according to his description, right-wingers claim in advance are bad, sectarian or untimely. At the same time, he stresses that he himself does not defend the Zagreb city government, but asks whether the right itself should move away from constant counter-positioning.\n\nŠarić agrees that the government should be praised when it achieves something good, but emphasizes that it would not occur to him to legitimize the government in matters with which he disagrees. He points out that if something objectively good is done, there is no reason for someone to block it merely because of who is in power.\n\nThe conversation also moves to a broader topic: Šarić believes that the first question in political reality should be whether something is objectively good for people, their lives, children and future, and only after that who these people are and what they previously advocated.",

     "subtitle": "From counter to counter: how politics reduces to constant opposition",
     "screenshot_description": "Graphic display of the left–right political spectrum and the number of new parties.",
     "content": "Marić connects Šarić’s views with the number of political parties: few parties, he claims, have a rounded ideological outlook, and every new party defines itself as the opposite of some other. When politics is built on counter-positioning, there is always someone to oppose, so parties continuously emerge.\n\nŠarić does not consider this an accurate explanation, but he introduces a philosophical idea that, in his opinion, explains this approach well. It concerns the critique of the politics of power advanced by certain authors on the threshold of postmodernity, and as an example he cites Michel Foucault. According to this understanding, there is no objective truth: there are only different camps and forms of power that present their actions as good.\n\nŠarić warns that such thinking leads to the question of what is good for society ceasing to be a subject of debate and becoming a question of who said it and how to fight against them. In this way, according to his thesis, politics turns into a struggle for supreme positions of power rather than a search for the common good.",

He explains the concept of **effective polarization** as polarization based on affect and emotions rather than on ideological consistency.\n\nThe conversation then turns to a concrete example, ecology, which in the next part of the discussion is used as an illustration of a broader principle. Marić announces that after ecology the conversation will expand to other questions considered important for consensus.",

     "subtitle": "How ecology became the brand of the green left",
     "screenshot_description": "Footage of a protest by environmental activists with banners about nature protection.",
     "content": "Marić asks how ecology became synonymous with the green left, given that it is something that has been universally present throughout history. Šarić believes this process occurred roughly from the eighties and nineties, and perhaps earlier, within the framework of the hippie movement and similar currents.\n\nAccording to his description, the green left began to emphasize love of nature, the need to preserve it, and criticism of man’s „corrupted“ relationship toward it. These ideas were initially general and beautiful, but the generations that advocated them gained political power. Then the question of environmental protection became a day-to-day political matter, and scientific theories about the catastrophic consequences of man’s disregard for nature became attached to it.\n\nŠarić argues that this approach has been branded for twenty to thirty years, and that today most listeners, when ecology is mentioned, probably think first of the green left. He concludes that ecology has become a brand, and the brand has become a means of survival.",

      "green left",
      "brand",

      "hippie movement"

    {
     "subtitle": "Preserving nature is not bad: objective good and motives for protection",
     "screenshot_description": "A family in nature: a child drinking water, picking fruit from a tree; an illustration of clean nature.",
     "content": "Šarić clarifies that the fact that the environment has become a brand of the green left does not mean that preserving the environment is in itself bad. On the contrary, it is, in his view, something that is objectively good by every principle, regardless of political affiliation. Everyone wants children to drink clean water, play in the meadow and pick fruit from trees, because they themselves have enjoyed these blessings.\n\nStarting from this assumption, Šarić proposes that we examine what the actual motive for preserving the environment is, whether from the perspective of the green left or from the perspective of the patriotic right. Marić follows on and confirms that these concepts can be discussed more precisely later.\n\nŠarić adds that the green left often takes up the value of the environment as the purposefulness of the system, and nature becomes something valuable in itself, almost like a deity. Such approaches, he argues, would often not accept the idea that an objective good exists.",

     "subtitle": "Nature as an end in itself: a critique of ecological biocentrism",
     "screenshot_description": "A depiction of a forest and landscape with the label „Gaja“ and the term „majka priroda“.",
     "content": "Marić asks how ecological movements view real pagans and their practices. Šarić replies that pagan practices were often animistic, that they explained everyday phenomena through nature and that they venerated it. He emphasizes that he is not an expert in this area, but believes there is a certain parallel between such a conception of nature and the contemporary ecological left.\n\nŠarić then warns of a problem in which nature becomes merely the purposefulness of the system, and man is not integrated into that story. As a consequence of such a view, he cites absurd claims, for example that the number of people on Earth should be reduced because people are carriers of a carbon footprint. Such ideas, in his view, represent a manifestation of a culture of death that flees from what should be the foundation of the desire to preserve the environment.",

     "content": "Šarić advocates that every environmental protection be primarily grounded in a healthy measure of anthropocentrism. This means that human dignity is recognized, that is, the value of the human person that is inherent to them and that cannot be taken away or conferred by the state or the international community. In his view, a large number of people accept such a value.\n\nStarting from this point, Šarić concludes that one cannot arrive at the claim that man as such is a carrier of a carbon footprint. Nature, in his view, exists so that man, in coexistence with it, may use what he needs without destroying it. The reasons for such an approach are the protection of future generations and the rights of other people who also need the possibility to use nature in the same way.",

     "content": "Marić mentions the concept of love of homeland, which is listed in the column as a notion that includes people, customs, culture and nature.      "screenshot_description": "A symbolic depiction of a local community and global institutions; a visual comparison.",
     "content": "Šarić explains that in the mentioned column he advocates the principle of **subsidiarity**, according to which the preservation of the environment is the responsibility of local communities. Local people who live in a particular environment recognize its value, consider it their home and want to preserve it for future generations.\n\nIn contrast, the approach of the green left, in his description, entails the creation of large international organizations, global plans and regulatory measures that are to be imposed globally. Šarić warns that international institutions are often under the influence of various interests.\n\nAs an illustration, he cites an example in which the thesis that meat consumption is unsustainable and should be eliminated would be imposed globally, because industrial cattle production creates a large carbon footprint. Although everyone can recycle, if large corporations use plastic for everything and anything, even for packaging everything living, individual recycling loses its meaning. That is why, Marić concludes, global bodies necessarily exist in ecology as well.\n\nŠarić agrees with this thesis and first points out that the division between anarchists and those who want to solve issues „from top to bottom“ has arisen within the left paradigm since its beginnings. This division, in his view, is not new.",

     "subtitle": "Bottom-up or top-down: a historical division",
     "screenshot_description": "A historical illustration of the First International with figures of Karl Marx and Mikhail Bakunin.",
     "content": "Šarić recalls that within the International the subject of disagreement was precisely the way of solving problems. On one side was Karl Marx, and on the other the anarchists led by Mikhail Bakunin, a Russian theorist who advocated an anarchist version of socialism. Both sides, in his description, advocated higher values, but they differed on whether the problem should be addressed through international organizations or through the anarchist action of people from below.\n\nŠarić points out that in history the advocates of international organizations prevailed, because they were more effective in practice. Anarchists, by the nature of their ideology, were not especially efficient at organizing.\n\nAs a practical solution for the contemporary world, Šarić proposes a paradoxical concept: there should be instances that are „from above“, but their primary principle must be to enable the action of those who are „from below“. As an example he cites the European principle of „unity in diversity“, according to which each state has the possibility of its own action and its own culture, while respecting shared international agreements.",

Šarić admits that he is not an expert in this area, but from public materials he believes it is a huge potential that the green left often ignores.\n\nAs an example he cites the situation in Croatia, in which Zelena akcija protested against the efforts of the Ministry of Economy to launch projects for the production of nuclear energy in the country. Šarić considers this absurd, because nuclear energy is often regarded as a sustainable and green form of energy, since it does not produce the emissions characteristic of burning fossil fuels.\n\nŠarić also recalls history: in the twentieth century nuclear energy was regarded as the future of humanity and a great promise, but that promise faded over time.",

He admits that certain risks exist, but claims that with responsible management nuclear energy is among the most efficient.",

     "screenshot_description": "A display of social networks, films and newspaper headlines spreading fears of catastrophes.",
     "content": "From the perspective of the sociology of risk, Šarić explains that the perception of fears in society, whether of climate change or of a nuclear catastrophe, largely depends on culture. This perception is influenced by the content consumed on social networks, in articles, on the radio, in films and in podcasts.\n\nWhen a certain topic, such as nuclear energy, becomes a daily matter, the individual feels a fear that is not rational and calculated, but a fear that culture has „sold“ to them as something they must be afraid of.\n\nAs an illustration, Šarić cites his own childhood experience with a documentary film about black holes, and mentions his fear of a possible catastrophe connected with experiments at CERN.      "screenshot_description": "A comparison of traffic accidents: a private car versus an airplane; a safety chart in frame.",
     "content": "Šarić gives an example of a statistical illogicality: in traffic in Zagreb it is much more dangerous to travel by private car than to fly by plane, yet people fear planes more. This, in his view, is a perception of fear that is created culturally, not a real risk.\n\nMarić adds that people also fear animals, such as spiders or snakes, which in these areas are a symbol of fear, although far more people are in fact harmed by animals that are actually more dangerous to them. Šarić also highlights the mosquito, which is responsible for hundreds of thousands of deaths a year in the world through the transmission of disease, but in Croatia is experienced only as a nuisance, because these diseases are not transmitted there.",

     "screenshot_description": "Children play in a meadow; in the background an orchard and a memory of a home garden.",
     "content": "Marić asks for a brief summary of why environmental protection is important, especially since the right side of the spectrum has most often shown interest in this topic. Šarić replies that generations born in the twentieth century enjoyed the blessings of natural life: walking in the park, playing on the grass, socializing in nature, drinking water from the tap and eating homegrown tomatoes from grandmother’s garden.\n\nFor this reason, in his view, we are obliged to enable future generations to have the same experience. We must not pollute and destroy the environment for the sake of large global promises of profit and GDP growth, nor because someone has been well paid to dispose of waste in our neighborhood.\n\nŠarić concludes that this is a common-sense question, not an ideological one, and that it would be absurd to ignore it merely because it was advocated by someone ideologically unacceptable.",

     "screenshot_description": "Šarić and Marić in the closing part of the conversation about ecology; a summary shot.",
     "content": "Šarić emphasizes that he advocates objective topics: we defend what is truly good, and we do not oppose something merely because someone advocates it. Struggle, in his view, may be a necessary means at certain moments, but it is not an end in itself and must not become a source of pleasure in opposing groups.\n\nMarić concludes that in this part of the conversation they have succeeded in defining the first national minimum on which agreement can be reached, and announces that the next questions will be put to the politicians who come to the show.",

     "screenshot_description": "Buildings of international corporations in a business district; a visual symbol of capital.",
     "content": "Šarić states that one of the issues on which the left and the right can agree is the negative effect of corporations on citizens. Although this is often considered a topic of left currents linked to workers’ rights, Šarić believes it is a social phenomenon that should be analyzed objectively.\n\nAs a tool for such an analysis he mentions the concept of **overarching capitalism**, which also appears in neoconservative circles of the right. According to his description, international corporations dictate the international labor market, command enormous amounts of capital and thereby shape people’s lives in unpredictable ways.\n\nŠarić concludes that democratically elected representatives should have the power to prevent corporations from acting to the detriment of the quality of everyday life of citizens.",

In his view, there should be a level of privilege granted to Croatian citizens in order to preserve the quality of life.\n\nMarić asks whether Šarić believes every political option must have a certain kind of protectionism toward the Croatian people and state. Šarić answers in the affirmative, but emphasizes that he does not want the people to use political catharsis by claiming that the state has not enabled them certain things. Every person, in his view, should try to secure what is vital to them, but whoever works in government must consider what level of protectionism would be appropriate.",

     "screenshot_description": "Shelves with domestic and imported products in a store; origin labels on packaging.",
     "content": "In defense of politicians, Marić points out that in Croatia there is a public consensus that everyone is at least somewhat in favor of protectionism, and that there are no prominent libertarians. He adds that this might also conceal the fact that party cadres need to be provided with employment, but he believes healthy protectionism is necessary.\n\nŠarić addresses market freedoms, that is, the freedom of movement of goods, people and capital. He warns that local producers may offer a higher-quality product, but find it difficult to compete on price with international producers who may have poorer criteria. The libertarian proposition, in his description, would be that people will rationally buy a cheaper product if it is better for their purpose.\n\nŠarić disputes this claim: people often do not have complete information about a product, so they do not know who makes the profit, under what conditions the product was made and what risks it contains. That is why, he concludes, supported local production and consumer awareness should be the principle rather than a completely free market.",

    {
     "subtitle": "The consensus that is missing: migration, foreign workers and citizenship",
     "screenshot_description": "Host Marin Marić and guest Petar Šarić in the studio, while Marić asks a question about consensus on migration.",
     "content": "Host Marin Marić opens a new topic with a question about migration and demography, for which he believes there should be at least one consensus about which there is no debate.
